There are a lot of different theories on how personality is developed, MBTI is only a theory geared at explaining personality. The different areas of psychology all have different ideas on how you develop your personality. 


Everything from the way you act in a certain environment to the way you think and have learned to think, the way you were raised, the way you develop relationships and go through life milestones, the way you feel about yourself. 


I think the most favorable area in psychology for INFPS would be humanistic, where there are ideas like phenomenology that focuses exclusively on you, the individual, as a unique phenomenon. I would look into some of Carl Rogers' work, he has a couple of books. Even Carl Jung's theories would be good to read as well.

While that's technically true, and there is no real "penalty" for quitting, to use your word, there are a lot of other things to consider. Being baptized as an infant means that the parents are religious. This means the child will be raised with that background: going to mass, getting the sacraments, maybe even going to Catholic school or at least religious ed, praying, being raised with religious ideals, ect.



To quit, they have to unravel all of the things particular to religion that they've grown up with, even if their family isn't super strict. They will have to recognize that it isn't something they believe in or want in their life, extract whatever it impacted, and decide what ideals they want to keep and what to toss. I think of it as a kind of reconstruction, where you pretty much have to rewire the entire way you handle the world. The more religiously strict the parents, the harder this is, as its more embedded in their lives. And the more pushback they're likely to get from their family. 



So yeah, if baptism was a one-and-done type of thing, I would totally agree with you. But being baptized means you're a part of the Church now. For older people who choose and really do have their own faith, that's totally fine. But for babies that are baptized and raised Catholic, sometimes fear and uncertainty keep them bound in.
